editorial.headline: A Clear PMA Route for Wholesale Fishery Trade in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale trade in fishery products and processed outputs is open to foreign investment nationally and remains available for PMA registration in Bali at the stated medium and large scales.
editorial.body:
Foreign investors can register this activity in Bali today. Its Bali position is not an exception made by ignoring the province’s PMA moratorium, but a result of the risk classification recorded for a large operation. Nationally, the activity is open to foreign investment up to a 100 per cent ceiling. In Bali, it is not blocked by the moratorium because the stated OSS risk at Besar scale is Medium-High/High, rather than one of the risk bands the moratorium catches. That makes this an open route with a higher-risk operating context clearly signalled in the record.

At its centre is wholesale trade in fishery products and related processing outputs, not a narrow single-commodity line. The scope takes in food fish, shrimp, crabs, oysters, pearls, shellfish, seaweed, sponges and frogs, as well as processed fishery products. It therefore accommodates a notably varied merchandise mix, from aquatic foods to particular marine and related goods, while holding to one commercial function: wholesale dealing. The inclusion of processed products is important: the category reaches beyond unprocessed items to fishery-derived preparations as they enter commercial trade.

Who may use it is defined by scale as well as scope. The record opens registration to Menengah and Besar businesses, placing this activity in the medium- and large-scale business context. For founders, the practical discipline is straightforward: frame the undertaking around the products actually named and the wholesale role actually stated. Its broad product vocabulary should not be treated as an invitation to blur the business description; the code’s coherence comes from dealing wholesale in these products, including their processed forms, at one of its specified scales. The two stated scales also prevent an overly casual reading of national openness: openness permits foreign ownership, but does not erase the scale labels alongside it.

At the national level, the “TERBUKA” status and 100 per cent maximum foreign ownership establish the baseline. Bali leaves that national ownership position intact for this activity. The province’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium applies to all Low and Medium-Low risk activities; this activity is recorded differently at the Besar scale, as Medium-High/High OSS risk. Accordingly, it is not blocked and carries the Bali status “OK_or_HIGHER_RISK”. That wording matters. It does not make the higher-risk classification disappear; it says that classification is precisely why the activity falls outside the stated moratorium. PMA registration is available in Bali because the stated large-scale risk band falls outside the moratorium.
